source.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of EEG Foundation Models via Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: W. Lehn-Schiøler; Magnus Ruud Kjær; Rahul Thapa; Magnus Guldberg Pedersen; A. Storgaard; N. Williams; Radu Gatej; T. Lehn-Schiøler; A. Brink-Kjær; S. Puthusserypady; S. Beniczky; James Zou; Lars Kai Hansen

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It tests whether replacing encoder activations with SAE reconstructions preserves task behavior, a conceptual test of V5 using classification AUROC rather than an explicit error-term analysis. It does not test the original residual-predictability or error-scaling measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper reports SAE-reconstruction substitution results for the normal/abnormal classification task. Those results are recorded below. It also reports SAE feature taxonomy, concept steering, and spectral-decoder results, but those do not measure the dark-matter error term. Hyperparameter-selection values are not outcomes on the claim.
record.test_reason: In a new setting (EEG transformers), it replaces layer activations with TopK-SAE reconstructions, dropping the error term, and measures retained normal/abnormal classification AUROC. This bears on whether the error carries function (V5). It has no random-error control, no loss measure, and no error-structure analysis, so V1–V4 and V6 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors treat AUROC preservation (within 0.017) under SAE substitution as a faithfulness check that the SAE keeps task-relevant structure. Their main conclusions concern the interpretability framework: the separable/entangled/dead taxonomy, steering-selectivity regimes including 'wrecking-ball' failures, and spectral decoding. They also note that separability does not guarantee selectivity.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses layer-wise TopK SAEs and tests activation-reconstruction effects on EEG classification AUROC. It does not use the original study's dark-matter residual analysis, linear predictability measurement, per-token error scaling, or same-context comparison across SAE sizes.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper evaluates reconstruction substitution across encoder layers. It reports per-layer bounds for all three encoders and notes LaBraM's layer-dependent performance pattern; it does not report faithfulness outcomes by SAE expansion rate.
record.problems: The reported faithfulness outcome is classification AUROC on one normal/abnormal task, not loss or a comparison against random errors of equal size. It does not measure the residual itself or isolate the effect of retaining that residual. Layer-wise results are summarized in text and figures rather than given as numerical values for each layer.
record.rows_left_out: Concept-steering sweeps and spectral-decoder results (Sections 4.2–4.5, Figures 3–6) were not extracted as claim rows: they concern deliberate concept interventions and decoded spectra, not the SAE reconstruction error or retaining that error. Expansion-rate results used for choosing operating points (Section 4.3, Figure 3) were also not claim outcomes.

untested.parts: Linear predictability of the SAE error from the input activation is not measured.
Per-token error norms, same-context failures across SAE sizes, and error persistence with scale are not measured. The expansion sweep is used only for the taxonomy.
No model loss is measured and no comparison with random errors of equal norm is made. AUROC preservation alone cannot show pathological-versus-random harm.
No split of the error into a linear part and a nonlinear part.

No circuit analysis or keep-vs-drop error comparison in steering. Steering is done on SAE-decoded embeddings without the error term and without a control that retains it. Only one coarse binary-task metric is used.
No comparison of SAE training objectives or architectures with respect to error size.

missing.what: Per-layer SAE-substitution AUROC values (especially LaBraM layers 1–3, where the drop is significant) are given only graphically
No reconstruction error / FVU / MSE values are reported for any SAE, so the size of the dropped error is unknown

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'challenges' is softened to 'limits_scope'. The faithfulness check is a single binary-task AUROC, which is insensitive to many representational losses. There is no random-error control and no loss measure. The models are small (d = 128–512) finetuned EEG encoders, not language models, and their ceiling AUROCs are near 0.95. The study does not engage with the dark-matter literature directly.

versions.untested_parts: No measurement of whether the SAE error is linearly predictable from its input activation.
No per-token error-norm predictability, comparison of error contexts across SAE sizes, or test of whether error persists with scale.
The paper evaluates classification AUROC after SAE reconstruction, but does not measure model loss or compare reconstruction errors with random errors of equal size.
No decomposition of error into learned-feature and nonlinear components, or test of whether either component resists further dictionary learning.

Tests task-AUROC retention after replacing activations with SAE reconstructions. Does not compare keeping versus discarding the error term in circuits or steering analyses, or assess other model behaviors.

Although SAE expansion rates are swept for feature-taxonomy selection, the paper does not test whether dark matter is caused by SAE training choices or shrinks with alternative architectures or end-to-end training.

relationships.condition: SleepFM (all 3 layers), REVE (all 22 layers), LaBraM layers 4–12; finetuned EEG encoders, binary normal/abnormal AUROC
relationships.reason: Dropping the SAE error costs at most 0.000–0.006 mean AUROC, statistically indistinguishable from the intact encoder (r1–r5). On this coarse, ranking-based task metric the error carries no measurable function. This qualifies V5 rather than refuting it for richer behaviours.
relationships.display_finding: AUROC was statistically indistinguishable from the intact encoder in these settings; reported mean losses ranged from 0.000 to 0.006, with 0.006 averaging all LaBraM layers.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: SleepFM (all 3 layers), REVE (all 22 layers), LaBraM layers 4–12; finetuned EEG encoders, binary normal/abnormal AUROC
source_check.reason: The text explicitly describes no statistically distinguishable AUROC loss in this condition group. The verdict rules assign challenges when the claimed effect is absent in the tested setting; untested richer behaviors do not justify limits_scope. Also, r5's mean Δ 0.006 averages all LaBraM layers and is not a mean for layers 4–12.

relationships.reason: Substitution causes a small but distinguishable AUROC drop (max Δ 0.017, r6). Some task function is lost, but much less than a 'meaningful share'.
relationships.display_finding: Early LaBraM reconstruction caused a small but statistically distinguishable AUROC decrease, reaching 0.017.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: The small LaBraM substitution loss, with maximum Δ 0.017 and recovery toward baseline at later layers, supports an incomplete effect. However, r6 reports an all-layer maximum; the text does not explicitly give early-layer significance tests or a threshold defining a meaningful behavioral share.

relation.reason: Replacing activations with SAE reconstructions and measuring classification AUROC directly bears on whether discarding reconstruction error loses task behavior.

tranche.reason: SAE reconstruction substitution supplies a result bearing on V5 in a new setting: fine-tuned EEG transformers evaluated on normal/abnormal classification.

source_check.notes: The native-head versus linear-probe inconsistency applies to every encoder. AUROC uncertainties summarize folds, whereas Mean Δ uncertainties summarize layers; preserved AUROC alone does not establish preservation of other behaviors.

statements.correction: SleepFM: layer-averaged AUROC 0.954→0.951. REVE: 0.944→0.944. LaBraM: all-layer mean Δ 0.006; maximum Δ 0.017. Substitutions are described as statistically indistinguishable for every SleepFM and REVE layer and LaBraM layers 4–12. Early-layer significance is not explicitly reported. Section 4.1 describes the native head; Table 2 and Figure 2 describe linear probes for all encoders.
statements.problem: The numerical summaries are correct. However, the text does not explicitly report statistical distinguishability for early LaBraM layers or for the maximum drop. The readout inconsistency concerns all three encoders. Under the verdict rules, the explicitly indistinguishable condition group warrants challenges.

statements.correction: LaBraM: maximum layer-wise AUROC drop 0.017; performance improves with substitution depth; substitutions are described as statistically indistinguishable from baseline from layer 4 onward. SleepFM: maximum drop 0.005 across 3 layers. REVE: maximum drop 0.006 across 22 layers. Early LaBraM per-layer significance results are not explicitly reported.
statements.problem: The maximum drop and later-layer indistinguishability are supported, but early-layer statistical distinguishability is inferred rather than explicitly established in the text.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: SleepFM, REVE, and LaBraM on the reported normal/abnormal test classification task
reader_labels.reason: SAE reconstruction substitution produces only small reported AUROC changes, which the authors describe as preserving task-relevant structure; see r1–r6. The paper does not test the explicit error-term comparison for circuits or steering.
